body_text: 3 Prerequisites Before You Automate Subscription Billing Key Takeaways Automated subscription billing systems that run independently from collections and cash application create unbilled receivables and corrupt deferred revenue schedules. Failed payments break revenue accounting by recording income you never collected while ASC 606 schedules treat uncollected charges as guaranteed revenue. Smart dunning with automated retry logic recovers failed charges before they corrupt revenue recognition, operating as an accounting fix rather than just a retention tool. Billing automation requires three integrated layers—invoicing, collections workflow, and cash application—in one closed loop to preserve accounting integrity. Most companies treat subscription billing as purely an invoicing problem, ignoring the downstream accounting consequences when payments fail to clear. Payment failures can create DSO numbers that misrepresent reality because the billing system records receivables that may never materialize into actual cash. Automated payment update workflows that handle expired cards and declined charges help prevent subscription lapses while keeping the general ledger aligned with actual collections. Related Video Watch: How to Build a Subscription Billing & Revenue Recognition Platform | Step-By-Step Guide by Intellivon What You Need to Know First Automating subscription billing without breaking revenue accounting means your billing system, collections workflow, and cash application engine must operate as one closed loop. When these three components run independently, you can end up with unbilled accounts receivable, distorted deferred revenue schedules, and DSO numbers that don’t reflect reality. Most businesses treat automatic subscription billing as an invoicing problem. They set up recurring charges, assume payments will clear, and move on. But when a payment fails, the entire accounting chain can break. Your billing system records revenue you haven’t collected, your GL shows receivables that may never arrive, and your ASC 606 recognition schedule treats uncollected charges as if they’re guaranteed income. The Three Prerequisites That Preserve Accounting Integrity Your billing automation must include these three layers to keep revenue data accurate. Automated collections with smart dunning catches failed payments before they corrupt your books. Automated retry logic and payment update workflows can push through declined charges, prompt customers to update expired credit cards, and send reminders so customers can fix their payment info before a subscription lapses. Recovering those failed charges is a revenue recognition fix. Every failed charge that goes unresolved creates a phantom receivable in your deferred revenue schedule, and ASC 606 doesn’t care whether you eventually collect it. The standard requires you to recognize revenue when performance obligations are satisfied, but if the customer never pays, your recognition schedule was wrong from day one. Cash application automation ensures payments match the correct invoices in real time. Manual matching introduces lag, and lag means your revenue subledger doesn’t reflect actual cash position. When your billing system auto-charges a subscription but your accounting team manually applies payments days later, you’re running two versions of truth. One version lives in your billing platform, the other in your ERP, and neither matches the bank account. Intelligent matching engines that connect payments to invoices at the envelope and item level can eliminate this drift. Revenue subledger integration turns your billing ledger into the single source of truth for both feature access control and ASC 606 compliance. Your billing system should produce clean journal entries that feed directly into your general ledger, not raw transaction logs that require manual interpretation. The same double-entry ledger that governs which customers can access your product is the ledger your auditors will review. If those two ledgers diverge, you’re either giving away product or recognizing revenue you didn’t earn. Why the Standard Billing-Only Approach Fails Billing automation without collections automation can create a silent revenue leak. Your system generates invoices, charges payment methods, and records revenue. But when cards expire, accounts close, or charges decline, the automation stops. Someone has to manually retry the payment, email the customer, or write off the receivable. During that gap, your revenue recognition schedule assumes the subscription is active and paid, and your books show deferred revenue that doesn’t exist. This gap is why unbilled AR builds up. Your billing system knows a charge failed, but your accounting system doesn’t update the recognition schedule until someone manually intervenes. The longer that intervention takes, the more your reported revenue diverges from collected cash. You may be able to skip this prerequisite if you’re running a low-volume operation and manually review every failed payment promptly. Otherwise, the manual reconciliation overhead can outpace your team’s capacity quickly. Why Automation Matters Manual subscription billing doesn’t just slow you down. It can quietly undermine your revenue accounting. When finance teams rely on spreadsheets to track recurring charges, they can create unbilled accounts receivable that sit unrecognized for weeks, leaving the general ledger showing revenue that hasn’t been collected and a Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) metric that loses meaning. Integrated billing and collections systems reconcile what was billed with what was actually collected, closing the gap between recognized revenue and cash received. The problem compounds when you consider scale. As subscription models grow in volume, traditional revenue assurance practices can struggle to detect anomalies in high-velocity transaction streams. Your billing team might process thousands of subscription renewals each month, but without automated reconciliation between your billing system, payment gateway, and revenue subledger, you’re flying blind. Every failed payment that gets manually logged creates another entry that needs manual correction in your ASC 606 recognition schedule. Who Actually Benefits from Billing Automation Finance teams see the most immediate relief. When subscription billing is automated, the monthly scramble to reconcile invoices against cash receipts shrinks. Your accounting team stops spending the first week of each month hunting down discrepancies between what was billed and what was paid. Companies above a certain revenue threshold are generally required to use accrual accounting for revenue recognition, and manual processes can struggle to maintain the audit trail required for compliance at that volume. The operational benefits extend beyond finance. Customer success teams benefit because automated dunning workflows can handle failed payments without human intervention. Retry logic that automatically prompts customers to update expired cards and retries declined payments can help reduce involuntary churn. In many cases customers don’t even realize a payment failed because the system resolved it before they noticed. What Breaks When Billing Runs Alone The failure point isn’t the billing automation itself. It’s treating automatic subscription billing as if it operates in isolation. Your billing system generates an invoice and records revenue. But if that payment fails, your revenue recognition schedule doesn’t automatically adjust. You’ve recognized revenue you didn’t collect, your deferred revenue balance is overstated, and your cash flow forecast is wrong. We see this play out in month-end close cycles. Finance teams that connect automated revenue recognition directly to their revenue subledger often report reduced close times and fewer audit corrections. The automation has to span the entire order-to-cash cycle. When billing, collections, and cash application operate as disconnected systems, you end up manually reconciling them anyway. Real-time revenue assurance has become important for subscription businesses because traditional revenue assurance practices can be inadequate for detecting anomalies in high-velocity transaction ecosystems. Your billing system might process a renewal correctly, but if the payment gateway returns a soft decline that your collections workflow doesn’t catch, that revenue never materializes. An accounting-led approach to anomaly detection—monitoring for deviations between contractual obligations and realized cash—only works when your billing, collections, and accounting systems share the same source of truth. The Revenue Leakage Nobody Tracks Unbilled accounts receivable is the silent killer. When mid-cycle upgrades require manual proration calculations, finance teams often defer the billing adjustment to the next cycle. That creates a gap where services were delivered but revenue wasn’t recognized. Multiply that across hundreds of subscription modifications per month and you’re looking at revenue leakage that doesn’t show up in standard reports. Usage-based pricing makes this harder. If your billing system can’t automatically mediate usage data—converting raw consumption events into accurate invoices—you’re either under-billing customers (revenue leakage) or over-billing them (disputes and refunds). Automated revenue management that handles usage data ingestion, proration logic, and ASC 606 compliance as a single integrated workflow reduces the manual reconciliation that creates reporting gaps. The larger point: automation matters because subscription revenue accounting requires recognizing income as services are delivered, not when customers pay. For example, a $1,200 annual subscription would be recognized as $100 per month over 12 months. If your billing system doesn’t automatically create that deferred revenue schedule, and your collections system doesn’t automatically adjust it when payments fail, you’re manually reconstructing your revenue position every month. That’s not just inefficient. It’s a compliance risk. Prerequisite 1: Aligning Subscription Contracts with Accounting Systems Misaligned contracts and accounting systems create a silent revenue leak. When your subscription terms live in one system and your recognition rules live in another, the numbers drift apart. Your automatic subscription billing engine charges customers on schedule, but if the contract’s performance obligations aren’t mapped to your accounting rules, you can recognize revenue you haven’t earned and defer revenue you should have booked. The fix starts with treating the contract as the source of truth for both billing and recognition. Automated subscription billing only preserves accounting integrity when the same contract data drives the invoice, the collections trigger, and the revenue subledger. Recurring billing collects money, subscription management handles plan changes and customer preferences, and the revenue subledger produces clean journal entries for ASC 606. These are three distinct layers, and conflating them is where alignment breaks. What Happens When Contracts and Accounting Systems Don’t Match Your billed amounts and your recognized revenue can tell two different stories, distorting deferred revenue and understating or overstating income. ASC 606’s five steps hinge on one thing: performance obligations stated explicitly in the contract. Miss that mapping, and a three-year software license paid upfront can get treated as current-period income instead of being deferred and recognized across 36 months. That’s a liability recorded as revenue. Regulators have scrutinized SaaS revenue recognition, and companies that fail to defer prepayments properly can face enforcement action. Map every contract’s performance obligations to a recognition schedule before the first charge fires, so billing and accounting draw from identical terms. Confirm your deferred revenue is treated as a liability until service is delivered, not booked as income on payment. Set recognition rules per pricing model. Tiered plans with feature enable require allocation across performance obligations; consumption-based pricing recognizes as metered events occur and get invoiced. How Do You Keep Alignment Automated Instead of Manual Your contract terms feed a shared ledger that both bills the customer and generates ASC 606 journal entries, removing the spreadsheet reconciliation step entirely. Structuring the accounting layer at the database level, rather than bolting it on at month-end, supports compliance. An immutable double-entry record documents the exact reason behind every balance change, providing the clear audit trail that regulatory reviews demand. Use a shared ledger so contract changes, mid-term upgrades, and cancellations flow to recognition automatically. Keep immutable transaction history rather than overwriting balance fields, so every recognition adjustment traces back to a contract event. Tie collections into the same loop. Failed dunning is a cash-application failure that can quietly corrupt deferred revenue schedules if it never reaches your accounting layer. Automated recognition first shortens the retrospective close and cuts audit corrections. The higher-value end state is continuous revenue assurance, where alignment is verified as transactions happen, not weeks later. If your subscription base is small and static, faster close is enough. Once plan changes and usage billing pile up, real-time alignment becomes more important. Prerequisite 2: Implementing Accurate Proration and Mid-Cycle Billing Proration breaks more revenue accounting than almost any other billing event. When a customer upgrades mid-month, downgrades on day 12, or adds seats on a Tuesday, your automatic subscription billing engine has to split the charge, recalculate the deferred revenue schedule, and hand the collections layer an accurate number to pursue. Miss any one of those, and your ASC 606 recognition can drift from what you actually earned. Most teams treat proration as an invoice-math problem. It isn’t. A prorated upgrade changes the performance obligation, which changes what you recognize and when. Automated subscription billing only stays clean when the proration calculation, the collections trigger, and the revenue subledger all read from the same event. Why Is Mid-Cycle Proration So Hard to Get Right Mid-cycle changes create partial periods that manual processes handle inconsistently. A finance team calculating proration in spreadsheets may round differently each time, book the wrong deferred revenue split, and leave the collections side chasing a stale figure. The root issue is timing precision. For example, a customer who upgrades from a $100/month plan to a $300/month plan on day 15 owes roughly $100 for the first half and $150 for the second half, but only if your system calculates exact days remaining. Round to the nearest week, and you can introduce an error that compounds across hundreds of accounts. Revenue recognition is about when a performance obligation is satisfied with a customer, and a mid-cycle upgrade satisfies a new obligation on a new timeline. The proration number and the recognition number are the same number, computed once. If they’re computed twice in two systems, they will disagree. Confirm your billing engine handles mid-cycle proration automatically, not through manual credit notes that bypass the recognition schedule. Verify every proration event writes a matching journal entry to the revenue subledger so recognized revenue tracks the actual partial period. Check that upgrades, downgrades, and add-ons each map to distinct performance obligations rather than a single flat adjustment. How Does Proration Connect Billing to Collections A prorated charge is only real once it’s collected. The gap between invoicing a partial charge and actually receiving it is where many recognition errors hide. If the collections layer doesn’t recover a failed prorated charge, that uncollected amount can quietly distort your deferred revenue. When payment methods fail on these mid-cycle adjustments, the resulting collection gap directly impacts the ledger. Automated outreach to resolve declined cards helps keep the recognition schedule honest and prevents uncollected proration from quietly turning into unbilled AR. Set dunning and retry logic to fire the moment a prorated charge fails, before it ages into the next cycle. Reconcile every prorated invoice against actual cash received, so recognized revenue never runs ahead of collections. Audit that partial-period credits and refunds reverse cleanly in both the ledger and the collections queue. What Should Your Proration Tooling Do Select systems that unify transaction records across your operational and financial tools. When a single ledger tracks both service delivery and financial bookings, proration ceases to be a reconciliation headache at month-end. Blixo automates recurring billing and integrates with accounting platforms like QuickBooks, Xero, Sage Intacct, and NetSuite to keep your ledger reconciled. For teams building out automated collections and dunning alongside recurring charges, check that your systems update together. Prerequisite 3: Establishing a Revenue Subledger for ASC 606 Compliance When your billing engine charges a customer, that transaction needs to land in a structured ledger that feeds both your collections workflow and your ASC 606 recognition schedule. Without a revenue subledger, you’re left with a billing system that knows what you charged, an accounts receivable report that knows what you’re owed, and a general ledger that treats both as separate universes. The gap between them is where unbilled AR hides, deferred revenue schedules drift, and compliance audits turn hostile. We see this break in practice when a customer upgrades mid-cycle. The billing system prorates the charge and sends an invoice. Collections retries the payment when the card fails. But if the revenue subledger doesn’t receive a unified event stream from both systems, your recognition logic runs on stale contract data. You might recognize revenue for a tier the customer left three weeks ago, or defer income you’ve already earned because the subledger never logged the upgrade. A revenue subledger built into the billing automation layer reduces that drift by treating every billing event—charge, retry, refund, proration—as an immutable ledger entry that updates the recognition schedule in the same transaction. What ASC 606 Requires from Your Revenue Subledger ASC 606 sets out a five-step framework: identify the contract, identify performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate that price, and recognize revenue as obligations are satisfied. The subledger is where steps four and five live. It holds the running allocation of each contract’s price across its performance obligations and posts the earned portion on the schedule those obligations dictate. If the customer downgrades or cancels, the subledger adjusts the remaining deferred balance and recalculates what you’ve earned to date. Without automated integration, that adjustment happens manually, often weeks after the event, leaving your financials out of sync with the actual services delivered. The accounting rules also require accrual consistency: you recognize revenue when you satisfy the obligation, not when you collect payment. That distinction becomes operational chaos when your collections layer runs independently. A payment retry weeks after the invoice date doesn’t change when you earned the revenue, but it does change whether the deferred balance should still sit in liabilities or move to bad debt. The subledger needs real-time visibility into both the billing event and the payment outcome to apply the correct treatment. Integrating automated revenue management so the subledger updates recognition schedules immediately as payment retries succeed or fail—rather than waiting for manual reconciliation—can reduce audit corrections and speed month-end close. Building the Subledger into Your Billing Automation A robust architecture designs the subledger directly at the database layer, using immutable, double-entry records to log every charge, credit, and adjustment. Storing a single running balance in a user table hides the history of why balances change, making it hard to reconstruct the performance obligations you satisfied. A transaction ledger that records each event separately lets you trace revenue recognition back to the original contract terms, which is exactly what an ASC 606 audit demands. We recommend integrating the subledger with your collections automation so failed payments trigger recognition adjustments without manual intervention. When a dunning workflow retries a declined card and succeeds, the subledger should log the successful charge and update the deferred revenue schedule in the same operation. When the retry exhausts all attempts, the subledger should flag the unbilled AR and move the deferred balance to a separate liability account or bad debt reserve, depending on your accounting policy. That closed-loop integration is how billing and collections can support ASC 606 compliance while improving financial reporting accuracy—every billing event flows into the subledger, and every collections outcome updates the recognition schedule. Tools and Best Practices for Revenue Subledger Management Use a strongly consistent relational database for your subledger to ensure data integrity and support audit trails. Document-based or key-value stores can make it harder to enforce accrual consistency across related transactions. Log every billing event as an immutable ledger entry rather than updating balances in place. This approach preserves the history needed to reconstruct performance obligations during an audit. Integrate the subledger with your dunning and cash application workflows so payment retries and declines automatically adjust deferred revenue schedules. Manual reconciliation introduces lag that distorts recognition timing. Align recognition policies with your contract performance obligations by mapping each subscription tier and add-on to a specific revenue category in the subledger. This helps you recognize revenue as obligations are satisfied, not just when invoices go out. Run regular compliance checks to verify that recognized revenue matches fulfilled performance obligations. Automated systems reduce errors, but periodic audits catch edge cases like contract modifications or pricing exceptions that require manual review. For businesses automating subscription billing at scale, the subledger can become the central nervous system that connects product access, collections, and revenue recognition. When those three layers read from the same ledger, your financials reflect what you actually earned, not just what you billed. Implementation and Next Steps Rolling out automation successfully comes down to sequencing. Turn on automatic subscription billing, then wire collections and cash application into the same event stream before you trust a single number in your GL. The mistake we see most often is teams flipping the billing switch first and treating collections as a cleanup task later. Automated billing only protects your revenue accounting if the collections layer runs in the same loop. Blixo’s automated collections send emails, text messages, phone calls, and letters to recover delinquent revenue, while its intelligent matching engine applies cash automatically, so the two layers stay connected. Unresolved payment failures directly distort the deferred-revenue schedule your recognition depends on. How Should You Sequence the Rollout Start with the data layer, not the invoice. Build the audit trail first, then layer billing, collections, and recognition on top of the same records. Design an immutable, double-entry record before writing any invoice logic. Updating a single balance column is risky because it erases the history of why a balance changed, and that history is exactly what your ASC 606 audit needs. Standardize your product catalog and pricing rules so proration, dunning, and recognition all read from one definition. Fragmented catalogs are a common root cause of mismatched charges downstream. Connect the payment gateway last. The gateway only collects money; the real work lives in the billing engine that decides what to charge and when to retry. What Should You Monitor After Go-Live Watch two metrics that expose whether billing and collections are actually reconciled: DSO and involuntary churn rate. When these move together, your billed revenue and collected cash are staying in sync. Track DSO weekly, not monthly. A rising DSO after automation often means dunning retries aren’t feeding back into your cash-application records. Monitor involuntary churn as a revenue-accounting signal, not just a retention stat. Failed payments that slip through dunning can inflate your recognized revenue against cash you’ll never see. Run regular reconciliation between the revenue subledger and the GL. Automated journal entries still need periodic audits to confirm recognition timing holds up. What Pitfalls Trip Up Most Teams The common failures are structural, not technical. They come from treating billing as a checkout flow instead of the system that connects product access, finance, and compliance. Don’t bolt recognition onto your month-end close. Build it at the database layer so the same ledger serves both operational tracking and financial compliance. Don’t skip usage mediation if you bill on consumption. Raw events have to convert into accurate invoices before they hit collections, or you’ll chase the wrong amounts. Skip full automation if your billing lives across disconnected spreadsheets today. Fix the source-of-truth problem first, or you’ll just automate the drift faster. If you’re moving from manual autopay setups, Blixo’s dunning and chasing tools handle card updates and customer notifications automatically. Get the loop closed, and your billing engine becomes the central nervous system your finance team can actually trust. Frequently Asked Questions Q: What is automated subscription billing? Automated subscription billing is a system that automatically charges customers on a recurring schedule, manages payment collection, and updates accounting records without manual intervention. It handles invoice generation, payment processing, retry logic for failed payments, and revenue recognition in one integrated workflow. Q: How does ASC 606 affect subscription billing? ASC 606 requires businesses to recognize revenue when performance obligations are satisfied, not when payment is received. For subscription businesses, this means revenue must be deferred and recognized over the subscription period. Automated systems track these performance obligations and adjust recognition schedules when customers upgrade, downgrade, or cancel. Q: What happens when a subscription payment fails? When a payment fails, your billing system records revenue you haven’t collected, creating unbilled accounts receivable. Without automated dunning and retry logic, these failed payments can distort your deferred revenue schedule and inflate your reported revenue. Smart retry workflows can attempt to collect the payment and update recognition schedules based on the outcome. Q: Why do I need a revenue subledger separate from my general ledger? A revenue subledger tracks the detailed allocation of contract prices across performance obligations and updates earned revenue as those obligations are satisfied. Your general ledger only sees the summary journal entries. The subledger provides the audit trail useful for ASC 606 compliance and helps keep your billing events, collections outcomes, and revenue recognition synchronized. Q: How does proration affect revenue recognition? Mid-cycle subscription changes create partial periods that require precise proration calculations. Each prorated charge represents a change in performance obligations, which changes what revenue you recognize and when. If your proration calculation and revenue subledger aren’t synchronized, you can recognize revenue that doesn’t match the actual service period delivered. Q: What’s the difference between billing automation and collections automation? Billing automation generates invoices and charges payment methods on schedule. Collections automation handles what happens when payments fail: retry logic, dunning workflows, payment method updates, and customer notifications. Both must run in the same loop to preserve revenue accounting integrity—billing automation alone can create phantom receivables when payments fail. Q: How long does it take to implement automated subscription billing? Implementation time depends on your starting point. If you’re migrating from spreadsheets with inconsistent contract terms, expect a longer effort to standardize your product catalog, build the revenue subledger, and integrate billing with collections. If you already have clean contract data and an accounting system that supports automation, implementation is typically faster. Q: Can I automate subscription billing if I have usage-based pricing? Yes, but you need usage mediation as part of your billing automation. Raw consumption events must be converted into accurate invoices before they reach collections. Without automated mediation, you’ll either under-bill customers (revenue leakage) or over-bill them (disputes and refunds). The mediation layer should feed the same revenue subledger that handles your subscription charges. body_text: Russ Havranek, MS, MBA Russ Havranek is the Executive Vice President of Commercial and Corporate Strategy. He was previously Vice President of Global Marketing and Business Development at Cytori Therapeutics. Mr. Havranek has over 28 years of leadership experience developing and commercializing diagnostic and therapeutic products at global, publicly traded, biopharma and medical device companies. His prior roles in marketing, strategy, business development, general management, and R&D focused on the oncology, rare disease, cardiology, and orthopedic markets. Management believes the non-GAAP information presented provides investors with additional useful information, but it is not intended to, nor should it be considered in isolation or as a substitute for the related GAAP measures. Moreover, other companies may define non-GAAP measures differently, which limits the usefulness of these measures for comparisons with such other companies. The Company encourages investors to review its financial statements and publicly filed reports in their entirety and not to rely on any single financial measure. Adjusted EBIT represents net income (loss) from continuing operations (a GAAP measure) before income taxes, interest expense, net, foreign exchange gain (loss), net, other expenses (e.g., gains/losses on extinguishment and modifications of debt, etc.), net, impairment losses, restructuring expenses, stock-based compensation, litigation expense (income), and certain other non-recurring items. Other non-recurring items are infrequent in nature and are not reflective of ongoing operational activities. Management believes that Adjusted EBIT is useful in providing period-to-period comparisons of the results of the Company's ongoing operational performance. Adjusted EBIT margin represents Adjusted EBIT divided by revenue. Adjusted EBITDA represents net income (loss) from continuing operations (a GAAP measure) before income taxes, interest expense, net, foreign exchange gain (loss), net, other expenses (e.g., gains/losses on extinguishment and modifications of debt, etc.), net, depreciation, impairment losses, amortization (service revenue, purchase accounting, and non-purchase accounting), restructuring expenses, stock-based compensation, litigation expense (income), and certain other non-recurring items. Other non-recurring items are infrequent in nature and are not reflective of ongoing operational activities. Management believes that Adjusted EBITDA is useful in providing period-to-period comparisons of the results of the Company's ongoing operational performance. Adjusted EBITDA margin represents Adjusted EBITDA divided by revenue. Adjusted EPS represents diluted earnings per share (a GAAP measure), excluding the effects of foreign exchange, impairments, amortization from purchase accounting, discrete tax items, and other significant non-recurring adjustments that are not reflective of on-going operational activities (e.g., gains/losses on sale of business, gains/losses on extinguishment and modifications of debt, etc.). Adjusted EPS is calculated using diluted weighted-average number of shares outstanding, including the impact of any potentially dilutive common stock equivalents that are anti-dilutive to GAAP net income (loss) per share but dilutive to Adjusted EPS. Management believes that Adjusted EPS is useful in providing period-to-period comparisons of the results of the Company's ongoing operational performance. Net debt is a non-GAAP financial measure that represents debt (a GAAP measure, calculated as long-term obligations plus short-term borrowings) minus capitalized debt issuance costs and cash and cash equivalents, including cash and cash equivalents classified as held for sale. Cash and cash equivalents, including cash and cash equivalents held for sale, are subtracted from the GAAP measure because they could be used to reduce the Company's debt obligations. Management believes that net debt is a useful measure to monitor leverage and evaluate the balance sheet. Net debt leverage is a non-GAAP financial measure that represents the ratio of Net debt as of a particular balance sheet date to Adjusted EBITDA for the last twelve months prior to such date. Management believes that net debt leverage is a useful measure to assess Brightstar's financial strength and ability to incur incremental indebtedness when making key investment decisions. Free cash flow is a non-GAAP financial measure that represents cash flow from operations (a GAAP measure) less capital expenditures. Management believes free cash flow is a useful measure of liquidity and an additional basis for assessing Brightstar's ability to fund its activities, including debt service and distribution of earnings to shareholders. Constant currency is a non-GAAP adjustment to certain financial measures that expresses current financial data using the prior-year/period exchange rate (i.e., the exchange rate used in preparing the financial statements for the prior year). Management believes that constant currency is a useful measure to compare period-to-period results without regard to the impact of fluctuating foreign currency exchange rates. title: World Energy Efficiency Day: The AI era’s defining challenge
summary: Discover how integrated power, cooling, and AI-enabled monitoring elevate data center energy efficiency and support scalable, responsible growth in the AI era.
body_text: World Energy Efficiency Day, observed each March 5, is a reminder that energy is not an unlimited input, and it must be managed carefully. It is a resource to be engineered deliberately from the start. That principle has never been more relevant to the data center industry. According to the International Energy Agency, global data center electricity use is expected to more than double, from approximately 415 terawatt hours (TWh) in 2024 to about 945 TWh by 2030 , roughly equivalent to Japan’s total annual electricity consumption. With rack densities exceeding 140 kilowatts (kW) , growth at this scale exposes a widening gap between compute demand and the efficiency of the systems built to support it. The question this day poses to the industry is straightforward: as AI workloads multiply and power grids strain to keep pace, is efficiency being treated as a design discipline? Capacity depends not only on how much can be secured, but on how well energy systems are designed and managed. Power supply is one side of the equation; how effectively energy is converted into usable compute inside the data center is the other. The first lever sits in the system architecture itself, particularly in how power and cooling are integrated from the outset. Designing efficiency into the system As data centers become more interconnected, separating power and cooling hardwires duplication into the design. Every conversion step—from fuel to electricity, from electricity to cooling—introduces loss and weakens control at the rack, where density and variability now concentrate. Integrating them removes those breaks in the chain and aligns generation, distribution, and heat removal from the start. As Chris Thompson, Vice President for Global Advanced Technology and Microgrid Solutions at Vertiv, says, “When power and cooling are treated as integrated system, efficiency becomes a design decision.” Figure 1. Power generation technology landscape for 3–10+ megawatt (MW) facilities with integrated power and cooling. Integration reduces redundant systems and captures usable heat, improving energy utilization , and tightening PUE. Source: Vertiv . Bring Your Own Power and Cooling (BYOP&C) applies that principle by engineering generation and cooling together so energy does double duty: first as conditioned power, then as usable thermal capacity. Waste heat can drive absorption cooling, reducing reliance on electric chillers and lowering auxiliary load. Coordinated electrical and thermal flows stabilize inlet temperatures and help improve power usage effectiveness (PUE), a measure of total facility energy relative to IT load, by reducing unnecessary conversions. The practical result: more of the energy brought on site ends up doing useful work. Making efficiency last Design sets the efficiency baseline; operations help determine how long it lasts. Over time, systems may drift. Equipment must work harder to deliver the same output, and energy use rises quietly in the background. Replacing existing systems is rarely realistic, so performance has to be protected within the infrastructure already in place. Preventive maintenance aims to bring systems back to their intended operating ranges before small deviations become standard practice. AI-enabled monitoring (see Video 1) adds continuous visibility into power use, load behavior, temperature trends, and component health. When equipment begins to draw more energy than it should, operators can act early, before incremental losses compound. Together, maintenance and monitoring turn energy efficiency from a design goal into a defined, actively managed part of daily operations. Video 1. Vertiv™ Next Predict brings AI-enabled monitoring to life — detecting anomalies early, before incremental losses compound. Inside a telecommunications collaboration achieving 20% energy savings Vertiv’s expanded collaboration with one of the major telecommunications operators in Spain includes maintenance and monitoring services to support energy efficiency. The agreement builds on a 2018 pilot at a core network site in Madrid that achieved an average 20% reduction in total energy consumption. Each site begins with a technical assessment that defines a targeted optimization plan with projected savings. As the program expands across Spain, it targets roughly 45 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in annual energy savings. Engineering energy for scale Energy efficiency also determines how far existing infrastructure can stretch before new capacity is required. Integrating power and cooling captures structural gains; maintenance and optimization services preserve them under real-world load. Architecture and operations together make efficiency a measurable, controllable outcome, not an assumption. As digital demand accelerates, long-term growth may depend on how deliberately energy is engineered, managed, and put to work. Learn how to power AI efficiently Explore the Vertiv™ AI Hub to see how AI is reshaping data centers with reference designs, efficiency strategies, and real‑world solutions you can apply today.

title: Gemini Markets: CLARITY Act Stalls As Senate Recess Looms
summary: With two days remaining before the Senate likely departs for the August recess, lawmakers have yet to file cloture for the CLARITY Act.
body_text: *Welcome to Gemini Markets, your read on crypto, prediction markets, and stocks, all in one place. Gemini Markets is your single weekly briefing on everything financial markets, reflecting Gemini’s push to become an all-in-one super app. This is the newsletter that will help inform you about what’s driving crypto and stock prices, tradfi market trends, and prediction market trends. * 📈 Crypto Markets Overview Still no vote on CLARITY Act as Senate recess looms: This procedural tactic would pave the way for a potential vote on long-awaited crypto market legislation, but there’s no indication yet it will hit the Senate floor over the next two days. The boxy design of older vehicles wasn’t just a stylistic choice; it also reflected the manufacturing technology available at the time. In the mid-to-late 20th century, automakers lacked the advanced tools we have today, such as computer-aided design (CAD). Without CAD, vehicle designers relied on simple, straight lines and flat surfaces that were easier to design and manufacture. Additionally, square shapes required fewer intricate molds, which reduced production costs. Beyond technological limitations, boxy shapes maximize interior space, headroom and cargo capacity, appealing to families and utility-focused buyers. Think of the classic Volvo 240 series sedan or wagon, and you’re about there. The boxy shape fell out of favor when new U.S. fuel economy standards were introduced in 1978, requiring automakers to improve mpg. Curved exteriors are more aerodynamic than boxy ones, so automakers began prioritizing this design to ensure they met the new standards. The boxy aesthetic saw a short resurgence in the early 2000s with vehicles such as the Nissan Cube and Scion xB. These compact cars embraced quirky, niche designs and provided excellent interior space for a small vehicle, catering to a younger audience seeking something unconventional and at a relatively low starting price. At this time, automakers could embrace the boxy designs of the past due to advancements in engine technology that enabled them to still meet fuel efficiency standards despite their less aerodynamic shape. While their popularity was relatively short-lived, they demonstrated the enduring appeal of boxy designs for drivers looking for individuality and practicality in their vehicles. Pros and Cons of Boxy Cars and SUVs Pros: Spacious Interiors: Boxy designs optimize headroom, legroom and cargo space, ensuring passenger comfort and practicality. Retro Appeal: The boxy shape evokes nostalgia, blending classic design elements with modern innovation. Versatility: Boxy vehicles cater to many needs, from family travel to off-roading adventures. Cons: Fuel Efficiency: Boxy shapes are less aerodynamic and can lead to lower fuel economy compared to streamlined vehicles. Wind Noise: Upright designs can increase wind resistance and more noise at highway speeds. Pedestrian Safety Concerns: Flat front ends with high grilles may pose increased risks in pedestrian collisions. For those embracing nostalgia or just looking for a practical design with ample interior space, the resurgence of the boxy design is a welcome diversion from the aerodynamic-focused vehicles of the past 15 to 20 years. They put each car through real-world testing and create detailed reviews of performance in a range of categories, from practicality and driving manners to cost-effectiveness and safety. We also analyze hundreds of thousands of used car listings on CarGurus.com to track which models consistently offer the highest percentage of best deals relative to how many are listed for sale. Then we factor in reviews from owners-people who actually live with these cars every day. Our proprietary Best Cars algorithm then creates a final Overall CarGurus rating combining expert scores, user reviews, and the percentage of listings that have earned the Good or Great Deal rating. This multi-pronged approach reveals not just which cars excel on paper, but which ones deliver satisfaction and value when you're ready to buy. title: The Heart Health Ingredient Many People Overlook: Why Added Sugar May Be a Bigger Risk Than You Think

body_text: Cardiologists Warn About the Hidden Impact of Added Sugar on Heart Health For years, saturated fat has been one of the first things people blame when discussing heart disease. While dietary fat can play a role in overall health, many cardiologists are now highlighting another common ingredient that deserves closer attention: added sugar. Dr Dmitry Yaranov, a cardiologist known for sharing heart health information with hundreds of thousands of followers online, has described added sugar as one of the biggest dietary concerns affecting cardiovascular health. According to his advice, the problem is not the natural sugars found in whole fruits or vegetables, but the large amounts of added sugar hidden in everyday foods and drinks. From fizzy drinks and sweetened coffee beverages to sauces, cereals, desserts, and processed snacks, added sugar has become a regular part of many modern diets. Research suggests that consuming too much added sugar may increase the risk of conditions linked to heart disease, including obesity, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and unhealthy cholesterol levels. How Added Sugar Can Affect the Heart The body needs glucose for energy, but excessive intake of added sugar can create problems over time. When people regularly consume large amounts of sugar, especially through sugary drinks and highly processed foods, it can contribute to metabolic changes that place stress on the cardiovascular system. A diet high in added sugar may contribute to: Increased inflammation in the body Higher blood pressure Greater risk of insulin resistance Increased levels of harmful blood fats Weight gain and obesity Higher chances of developing type 2 diabetes These factors are closely connected with cardiovascular disease, one of the leading causes of death worldwide. Unlike naturally occurring sugar in foods such as apples, berries, and milk, added sugar often provides calories without important nutrients such as fibre, vitamins, and minerals. This is why health experts often describe sugary foods and drinks as sources of "empty calories." Sugary Drinks and Heart Disease Risk One of the biggest sources of added sugar is sugar-sweetened beverages. Soft drinks, energy drinks, sweetened teas, and many packaged juices can contain large amounts of sugar in a single serving. A study from researchers at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health examined the relationship between sugary drinks, physical activity, and cardiovascular disease risk. The research suggested that drinking sugar-sweetened beverages regularly was associated with a higher risk of heart disease, even among people who exercised regularly. The findings highlight an important message: exercise is extremely beneficial for heart health, but it may not completely cancel out the negative effects of a diet consistently high in added sugar. The Link Between Added Sugar and Heart Disease Death Risk Research published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2014 examined the relationship between added sugar intake and cardiovascular deaths. The study followed thousands of adults over many years and found that people who consumed a higher percentage of their daily calories from added sugar had a significantly increased risk of dying from heart disease. The researchers observed that the risk increased as added sugar consumption increased. The association remained even after considering factors such as physical activity, body weight, and other lifestyle factors. This does not mean that eating a small amount of sugar will immediately damage the heart. Instead, it shows that consistently consuming excessive amounts over many years may increase cardiovascular risk. Where Is Added Sugar Hiding? Many people consume more added sugar than they realise because it appears in foods that may not seem like desserts. Common sources include: Soft Drinks Fizzy drinks are among the largest contributors of added sugar in many diets. A single can can contain several teaspoons of sugar, quickly pushing daily intake above recommended levels. Cakes, Biscuits, and Pastries Sweet baked foods often contain a combination of sugar, refined carbohydrates, and fats. Eating these foods frequently can contribute to excessive calorie intake. Breakfast Cereals Some breakfast cereals marketed as healthy options can contain significant amounts of added sugar. Checking nutrition labels can help identify lower-sugar alternatives. Sauces and Condiments Ketchup, barbecue sauce, sweet chilli sauce, and salad dressings can contain surprising amounts of added sugar. Flavoured Yoghurts Although yoghurt can be a nutritious food, some flavoured varieties contain high levels of added sugar. Plain yoghurt with fresh fruit is often a lower-sugar choice. How Much Sugar Should You Eat? Health guidelines recommend limiting free sugars, which include added sugars and sugars naturally released from fruit juices. According to NHS guidance, adults should consume no more than 30 grams of free sugars per day, which is around seven teaspoons. Children have lower recommended limits depending on their age: Children aged 7 to 10: no more than 24 grams daily Children aged 4 to 6: no more than 19 grams daily Children aged 2 to 3: no more than 14 grams daily Reducing added sugar does not mean eliminating all sweet foods forever. Small changes can make a meaningful difference. Simple Ways to Reduce Added Sugar Intake Making healthier choices does not require a complete diet overhaul. Some practical steps include: Replace sugary drinks with water, sparkling water, or unsweetened drinks Choose whole fruit instead of fruit juice Read food labels and compare sugar content Select plain yoghurt instead of flavoured versions Reduce sugar added to tea and coffee gradually Cook more meals at home where possible Choose snacks with protein and fibre to stay fuller for longer The Bigger Picture: Protecting Your Heart Heart health depends on many factors, including genetics, physical activity, sleep, stress levels, smoking habits, and overall diet quality. No single ingredient alone determines whether someone develops heart disease. However, evidence continues to show that reducing excessive added sugar intake can be an important part of a heart-friendly lifestyle. A balanced diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, lean proteins, and healthy fats, combined with regular movement and medical check-ups, remains one of the strongest approaches to protecting cardiovascular health. The key message from cardiologists is not that sugar must disappear completely, but that hidden added sugar deserves more attention. By understanding where it appears and making small changes, people can take practical steps toward supporting long-term heart health. Sources Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health research on sugar-sweetened beverages and cardiovascular disease risk. JAMA Internal Medicine (2014), "Added Sugar Intake and Cardiovascular Diseases Mortality Among US Adults." British Heart Foundation guidance on free sugars and heart health. NHS guidance on daily recommended limits for free sugars. Nature Medicine research on global health impacts associated with sugar-sweetened beverages. Disclaimer This article is for informational purposes only and does not replace professional medical advice. Dietary needs vary between individuals. If you have concerns about heart health, diabetes risk, or changes to your diet, consult a qualified healthcare professional.

title: What’s new in Stardex: August 2026
summary: An autonomous ATS + CRM for executive search firms built for the age of AI.
body_text: This month, we’ve made Stardex more collaborative, context-aware, and easier to use. AI search can now ask clarifying questions and account for your priorities, while the new Team Knowledge Base gives Ask Dex access to the institutional knowledge that makes your firm unique. We’ve also added smarter email workflows, better company relationship mapping, and several quality-of-life improvements across campaigns, reports, integrations, and more. Here’s what’s new in Stardex. AI search is now agentic Our internal AI search used to be one-shot but now it works more like a researcher: it’s collaborative and asks you clarifying questions when your criteria are ambiguous. It allows you to prioritize the criteria, and we have updated the candidate ranking to be more relevant and the UX to be a bit cleaner. Team Knowledge Base Every firm has context that lives in people's heads. This client always passes on candidates without PE backing, that company's comp bands run low - or maybe it’s some other secret sauce only your team knows. You can now save that as team memory, and Ask Dex pulls the relevant bits automatically when you're working a search. In beta now! Attachments in campaigns and email templates For all the folks that prefer attaching PDFs to their candidate outreach, this is what you’ve been waiting for! You can now attach PDFs and Word docs to your campaigns, instead of pasting in links. This is supported in one-off email templates as well. Email forwarding assistant Forward an email into Stardex and we'll figure out who it belongs to and file it on the right record, no manual matching. Useful for the threads that happen outside your connected inbox, like when a client loops you in from a different address. Admins can turn it on for the team in settings, and available on the pro tier. We are still testing this, so would love to hear feedback. Company network On any company page you'll now see a network view of everyone in your database who has worked there and where their time overlapped. It's the fastest way to find a backchannel reference or figure out who can make an intro into an account you're trying to break into. Quality of Life • Goals are now in Reports . Set targets by metric, for the team or per person, and track progress against them. • Campaign sending got safer : per-mailbox daily send limits, plus min and max gap settings so your outreach paces out naturally instead of firing all at once. • Metaview x Stardex Integration: We’ve shipped a native integration with Metaview! Transcripts and call summaries now automatically pull into Stardex candidate profiles. Here’s a guide on enabling the integration. • You can now block a campaign from moving forward until a task is done , useful when a step needs a human to actually do something first. • Schedule rejection emails instead of sending them the moment you reject someone. • The Chrome extension now shows your list of tasks , so you can breeze through them much quicker. • API keys now support scopes , so you can hand out access that's limited to what an integration actually needs. • Download a job share as PDF or Word , and share links now have branded thumbnails. • Set org-wide default column layouts and reorder custom fields so everyone starts from the same view.

body_text: NI Holdings, Inc. Reports Results for Second Quarter Ended June 30, 2026 August 7, 2026 PDF Version FARGO, N.D., Aug. 07, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- NI Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ: NODK) announced today results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026. Summary of Second Quarter 2026 Results (All comparisons vs. the second quarter of 2025, unless noted otherwise) Gross premiums written of $107.2 million compared to $111.8 million in the prior year quarter. This decrease was driven by Non-Standard Auto (-98.9%) reflecting the continued impact of the Company’s strategic decision to exit the majority of the segment, as well as a decline in Private Passenger Auto (-8.0%) due to lower renewal premiums and new business in South Dakota and Nebraska, partially offset by increased new business in North Dakota. These declines were partially offset by All Other (+46.7%) due to increased assumed premiums from participation on catastrophe reinsurance programs of certain farm bureau insurance companies, and Crop (+8.8%) due to increased new business. Combined ratio of 107.7%, versus 125.1% in the prior year quarter. The improvement was primarily driven by lower catastrophe losses, favorable prior year development on loss reserves in Non-Standard Auto during the current year quarter compared to unfavorable prior year development in the prior year quarter, and improved growing conditions in Crop, partially offset by higher non-catastrophe weather-related losses in Home and Farm. Total pre-tax catastrophe loss of $15.0 million for the quarter, which was below our reinsurance retention and adversely impacted the second quarter and year-to-date loss and loss adjustment expense ratios by 23.1 and 12.5 percentage points, respectively. This compares to total pre-tax catastrophe loss, net of reinsurance, of $20.0 million and $3.3 million of related reinstatement premiums in the prior year quarter, which adversely impacted the prior year quarter and prior year-to-date loss and loss adjustment expense ratios by 30.2 and 15.7 percentage points, respectively. Net investment income of $2.8 million, down 10.7% from the prior year quarter, primarily due to a lower average fixed income portfolio balance. Basic earnings per share of $0.01, compared to basic loss per share of $(0.57) in the prior year quarter, reflecting improved profitability for the quarter. These strong quarterly results reinforce our strategic trajectory, setting a solid foundation for the remainder of the year and keeping us on the path toward creating lasting value for our shareholders.” Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Filings The Company’s Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q and latest financial supplement can be found on the Company’s website at www.niholdingsinc.com . The Company is a North Dakota business corporation that is the stock holding company of Nodak Insurance Company and became such in connection with the conversion of Nodak Mutual Insurance Company from a mutual to stock form of organization and the creation of a mutual holding company. Immediately following the conversion, all of the outstanding shares of common stock of Nodak Insurance Company were issued to Nodak Mutual Group, Inc., which then contributed the shares to NI Holdings in exchange for 55% of the outstanding shares of common stock of NI Holdings. Nodak Insurance Company then became a wholly-owned stock subsidiary of NI Holdings. title: We've Raised $150 Million in Series C Funding to Build Enterprise Superintelligence
summary: New funding led by Prysm Capital and co-led by Eurazeo will accelerate our global growth as we expand our engineering, deployment and go-to-market teams
body_text: We're excited to share that we've raised $150 million in Series C funding, led by Prysm Capital and co-led by Eurazeo. Existing investors a16z, Base10, and Y Combinator are doubling down, joined by strategics including Koch Disruptive Technologies (KDT), Kfund, Orange, T.Capital (Deutsche Telekom), Bankinter, Endeavor Catalyst, and Wave-X. This round values us at $1.2 billion post-money, bringing our total funding to around $200 million as we enter a new stage of growth, deploying our AI agents across more of the mission-critical work enterprises can't afford to get wrong. The Real Economy, At Scale We now work with more than 150 enterprise customers, including DHL, Kuehne + Nagel, Naturgy, Repsol, and Uber, and we've grown 5x since raising our Series B late last year. After first proving our platform in logistics, one of the world's most operationally demanding industries, we're expanding across the supply chain as well as into insurance, energy and utilities, telecommunications, airlines, and other sectors where business-critical work still depends on manual coordination across fragmented systems. Why We're Raising This new funding will accelerate investment in our platform, including expanded AI capabilities, enterprise integrations, and the infrastructure required to deploy AI agents at scale. We'll also continue growing our engineering, deployment, and go-to-market teams globally to support increasing demand from enterprises across industries. title: Paneles solares Puente Alto
summary: Reduce tu cuenta de luz con paneles solares en Puente Alto. Descubre cuánto puedes ahorrar, qué factores influyen en la instalación y cómo elegir el sistema ideal para tu hogar.
body_text: Si estás pensando en paneles solares en Puente Alto, y vives ahí, hay algo que probablemente no sabes todavía, y que puede cambiar cómo se hace el trámite: la comuna tiene su propia empresa distribuidora de electricidad, distinta a Enel o CGE. Vamos por partes. Puente Alto es la comuna más poblada de Chile, con casi 600.000 personas, casas construidas en distintas décadas, techos de todo tipo, y una cuenta de luz que, como en el resto del país, no ha dejado de subir en los últimos años. Quién vende la luz en Puente Alto (y por qué importa) La mayoría de la gente asume que en la Región Metropolitana la electricidad la reparte Enel. En Puente Alto, no necesariamente. Una parte importante de la comuna es abastecida por la Empresa Eléctrica Puente Alto (EEPA), una compañía local con más de 100 años de historia que atiende a decenas de miles de clientes residenciales, comerciales e industriales dentro de su zona de concesión. Otras zonas de la comuna sí son atendidas por Enel o CGE, dependiendo de dónde esté tu casa exactamente. ¿Por qué te tiene que importar esto? Porque el trámite de Net Billing, el que te permite instalar el medidor bidireccional y descontar tus excedentes de la boleta, se hace con TU distribuidora específica, no con "la eléctrica de Santiago" en general. Si tu instaladora no revisa esto antes de cotizar, puede terminar coordinando con la empresa equivocada, y eso sí te atrasa el proyecto. Antes de cotizar en cualquier parte, revisa tu boleta de luz: ahí dice exactamente quién es tu distribuidora. Cuánto sol le pega a Puente Alto (spoiler: bastante) Puente Alto está en la cuenca de Santiago, con niveles de radiación solar que están entre los mejores del país para generación residencial. La Región Metropolitana en general recibe alrededor de 4,5 a 5,5 horas de radiación solar en condiciones óptimas para la producción fotovoltaica, aunque este valor varía según la estación. Eso no es un dato decorativo. Es literalmente el insumo principal de tu sistema: más horas de sol, más energía generada por cada panel instalado, mejor retorno de tu inversión. Lo que sí varía casa por casa es la orientación del techo y las sombras. Un techo orientado al norte sin árboles ni edificios cercanos que tapen el sol va a generar bastante más que uno orientado al sur con una sombra de la casa del vecino cayendo encima cada tarde. Esto no se estima a ojo, se mide. Cuánto podrías ahorrar realmente Vamos con números, no con promesas vagas. En promedio, los clientes de RUUF en todo Chile ahorran $103.158 al mes en su cuenta de luz. Eso no significa que tu caso específico vaya a ser exactamente ese número, depende de tu consumo, tu techo y tu distribuidora, pero sirve como referencia real, no inventada. Un ejemplo con números redondos para una casa típica de Puente Alto: Consumo mensual: 350 kWh Cuenta de luz actual: aproximadamente $75.000-$85.000/mes según tarifa vigente Sistema solar dimensionado para cubrir la mayor parte del consumo: entre 6 y 8 paneles Nueva cuenta de luz: cerca del cargo fijo mínimo, en la mayoría de los meses Ahorro anual estimado: sobre $700.000 La inversión se suele pagar entre 5 y 8 años, y los paneles siguen generando energía por hasta 25 años. Haz la cuenta: dos décadas largas de ahorro después de recuperar lo invertido. Estos números son referenciales, tu caso real se calcula con tu consumo específico, no con un promedio. Puedes ver el detalle de cuánto cuesta instalar paneles solares en Chile para entender qué factores mueven el precio hacia arriba o hacia abajo. Lo que nadie te cuenta antes de instalar en una comuna con distribuidora local Trabajar con una distribuidora más pequeña y local como EEPA tiene un lado bueno y uno menos bueno, y conviene que los sepas de entrada. Lo bueno: al ser una empresa más chica, en algunos casos los procesos de coordinación pueden ser más directos que con una distribuidora gigante que atiende a millones de clientes en todo el país. Lo que hay que vigilar: no todas las distribuidoras tienen el mismo nivel de digitalización de sus procesos. Algunos trámites que en zonas atendidas por las distribuidoras más grandes ya están bastante automatizados, en distribuidoras más pequeñas pueden depender más de gestión manual. Esto no es necesariamente peor, pero sí es distinto, y tu instaladora debería saber manejarlo sin que a ti te toque perseguir papeles. Lo importante es que quien te instale conozca bien el proceso completo de Net Billing en Puente Alto específicamente, no un proceso genérico copiado de otra comuna. Errores comunes al cotizar paneles solares en Puente Alto No revisar quién es tu distribuidora real antes de cotizar. Asumir que es Enel cuando en realidad es EEPA (o viceversa) puede generar confusión innecesaria en el trámite. Dimensionar el sistema por la factura de un vecino, no por tu consumo real. Cada casa tiene un patrón de consumo distinto, aunque estén en la misma cuadra. Ignorar las sombras del entorno. Un árbol grande o un edificio vecino puede tener más impacto en tu generación del que imaginas, merece un análisis, no una estimación a ojo. No preguntar por el tiempo real del trámite completo , no solo el de la instalación física. El proceso de aprobación y cambio de medidor toma semanas, no días, independiente de qué tan rápido sea instalar los paneles solares en sí. Preguntas frecuentes sobre paneles solares en Puente Alto ¿Cualquier casa en Puente Alto puede instalar paneles solares? En términos generales sí, siempre que el techo tenga suficiente espacio libre de sombras y esté en condiciones estructurales adecuadas. La forma de saberlo con certeza es con una evaluación de tu dirección específica, no con una regla genérica. ¿Cuánto tiempo toma todo el proceso, desde cotizar hasta tener el sistema funcionando? En promedio, entre 2 y 4 meses considerando diseño, aprobación con tu distribuidora, e instalación. La instalación física en sí se hace en uno o pocos días; lo que toma más tiempo es la tramitación administrativa. ¿Necesito baterías para que mi sistema funcione en Puente Alto? No necesariamente. La mayoría de los sistemas residenciales funcionan conectados a la red (on-grid) sin batería, y siguen ahorrando en la cuenta igual. Las baterías son un costo adicional, útil si además quieres tener respaldo durante cortes de luz. ¿Quieres saber cuál es la diferencia entre on-grid y off-grid? Puedes revisar esta guía sobre qué es el grid . ¿El ahorro promedio de $103.158 aplica igual en Puente Alto que en otras comunas? Es un promedio nacional de clientes RUUF, no un número fijo por comuna. Tu ahorro específico depende de tu consumo actual, tu tarifa, y cuántos paneles caben bien en tu techo, por eso una cotización personalizada da un número mucho más útil que un promedio. La decisión, con los números sobre la mesa Puente Alto tiene buen sol, un parque de casas enorme, y una particularidad administrativa, su propia distribuidora eléctrica local, que vale la pena tener clara antes de cotizar en cualquier parte. El ahorro es real y medible, no una promesa de marketing: se calcula con tu consumo, tu techo y tu distribuidora específica, no con un número genérico sacado del aire. ¿Quieres saber cuánto podrías ahorrar con paneles solares en tu casa? Cotiza gratis online con RUUF : en minutos ves cuántos paneles necesita tu casa, cuánto ahorrarías y las opciones de financiamiento.

title: Nakamoto Launches Intelligence 2027, a New Flagship Event for the AI Economy
summary: A Defining Forum for the Builders, Investors, and Institutions Driving the Future of AI
body_text: A Defining Forum for the Builders, Investors, and Institutions Driving the Future of AI NASHVILLE, TN – August 12, 2026: Nakamoto Inc. (Nasdaq: NAKA) (“Nakamoto” or the “Company”) today announced the launch of Intelligence 2027 (“i27”), which is anticipated to be an annual forum for leaders across the artificial intelligence economy. The inaugural flagship event will take place on April 22 – 23, 2027 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco, California bringing together founders, investors, enterprise executives, developers, policymakers, creators, and institutions shaping the next era of AI, from frontier models and infrastructure to enterprise adoption, consumer products, capital markets, and more. The launch of i27 marks Nakamoto’s expansion of its industry leading events platform into one of the world’s largest and fastest-growing technology markets. Through its subsidiary BTC Inc., the Company has spent more than a decade building The Bitcoin Conference into the marquee annual gathering of the global Bitcoin ecosystem. i27 will apply that same operating model to AI through high-caliber programming, culturally relevant speakers, and platforming the most important conversations to allow all levels of attendees access to learning more about a technology that has and will continue to shape our future. AI is no longer solely a software cycle. It is a revolution touching every corner of the global economy. i27 is designed to reflect that breadth, covering the full AI landscape, including business adoption, consumer products, developer tools, robotics, enterprise software, media and creative tools, investment, policy, education, security, infrastructure, and the cultural shifts created by increasingly capable intelligent systems. The event is expected to convene the full range of participants driving and responding to that transformation, from the companies building frontier systems to the enterprises deploying them, the investors backing them, and the policymakers governing them. “We view i27 as a natural extension of the capabilities we have built within our events and media business. Artificial intelligence represents a massive and rapidly evolving market, and we believe there is a significant opportunity to create a premier annual gathering for the companies, investors, developers, and institutions driving its growth. Our team has a proven track record of building industry-defining events, and we are excited to bring that experience to one of most consequential technological shifts of our time.” says David Bailey, CEO and Chairman of Nakamoto. Additional details regarding i27, including programming themes, speakers, sponsors, and ticket availability, will be announced in the coming months. For more information, visit i27.ai .
